edges.effect_quant: The signal is not dramatic, but pooled cohort evidence repeatedly shows higher stroke risk once weekly working time reaches 55 hours or more.
edges.mechanism: Very long working hours likely increase stroke risk through sustained sympathetic activation, sleep restriction, poorer recovery, and spillover into blood pressure and metabolic strain. The dose-response pattern in pooled cohorts is more persuasive than any single national dataset.
edges.summary: The best anchor is the WHO/ILO stroke review in Environmental International, which found a moderate increase in incident stroke among people working at least 55 hours a week. The earlier Lancet meta-analysis points in the same direction, even though not every national cohort reproduces the pooled estimate equally well.
edges.caveats: Exposure measurement is imperfect and long hours correlate with job grade, shift timing, and baseline health. The evidence is stronger for incident stroke overall than for every subtype separately.

evidence.citation: Descatha A et al 2020 Environ Int
